title: About
text:
Hello everyone, and welcome to my webpage. I am a political scientist whose academic interests revolve around the relationship between money and politics with a particular focus on post-Soviet polities. My research focuses on both the effects of party and campaign finance regulations on political corruption and party competition as well as forces shaping the content and restrictiveness of political financing regimes.
  I am currently a Research Fellow in the CONSULTATIONEFFECTS project at the Department of Comparative Politics, University of Bergen. The CONSULTATIONEFFECTS investigates the linkage between stakeholder consultations and policy making in the European Union. Prior to this position, I was a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral Researcher at the School of Law and Government, Dublin City University. During the Marie Curie Fellowship, I investigated the effect of direct public funding of political parties on political corruption within the framework of the Horizon2020 project “Does Public Funding Matter? The Effect of State Subsidies to Political Parties on Political Corruption”.

title: Replication of Hummel, C., Gerring, J., Burt, T. (2021): ‘Do Political Finance Reforms Reduce Corruption?’
text:
In this blog post, I discuss and replicate Hummel et al. (2021). Their article is perhaps the most ambitious effort to estimate the effect of public funding on political corruption in terms of geographical and temporal coverage. The article stands out from other cross-national studies on the relationship between party financing and corruption due to the authors’ efforts to construct a Political Finance Subsidy Index (PFSI) covering “175 countries and 115 years, generating 12,380 country-year observations” (Hummel et al., 2021, pag., 6), which is truly impressive. However, unlike Casal Bértoa et al. (2014), who rely on a public funding measure reflecting somewhat closer the level of funding political parties receive from the state, PFSI represents a much weaker measure. It represents an aggregate measure of five dichotomous (no = 0, yes = 1) indicators.

title: Direct public funding of political parties: between proxy measures and hard data (2)
text:
In the previous blogpost, I argued that binary indicators of party funding such presence vs absence of public funding, donation or spending caps are poor proxies to use in research assessing the impact of financing regulations on political competition, corruption, or other phenomena of interest. The same applies to aggregate indexes of party and campaign funding, which combine different regulatory dimensions (donation caps + spending caps + public funding + transparency) and derive a composite measure through their addition or some alternative procedure. Since comparative cross-national data of party and campaign funding is difficult to obtain, there is a tendency to use expert-based evaluations of different aspects, such as the significance of public funding for the election campaign of parties and candidates or the fairness in the distribution of campaign subsidies. Yet, the critical challenge these measures face is their validity – how accurately expert assessments capture the actual situation. The analysis of two such indexes against real data reveals a rather low validity. Figure 1 presents the results.1 In the left-hand panel, I correlate my data on the public funding level (Lipcean, 2021) with the expert scores average for the question from the Varieties of Democracy dataset “Is significant public inancing available for parties’ and/or candidates’ campaigns for national office?” (ordinal scale ranging from 0 (no subsidies) to 4 (significant subsidies)) (Coppedge et al., 2020; Coppedge et al., 2021). In the right-hand panel, I correlate my data on the legal requirements to get access to campaign subsidies with the expert scores average from the “Electoral Integrity Project” for the question “Parties/candidates had equitable access to public political subsidies?” (ordinal scale ranging from 1 (strong disagreement) to 5 (strong agreement)) (Norris & Grömping, 2019a, 2019b). As one may notice, the relationship between actual indicators of public funding and expert assessments produce a considerable mismatch, indicating that expert judgements must be treated cautiously in research on political financing.
Figure 1: Relationship between expert scores, subsidy level and payout threshold
The above examples show that, as the regulation-based indicators or composite measures, expert evaluations are not valid proxies for the public funding mechanism. Hence, the question is whether one can identify better proxies that can be used by scholars in comparative research assessing the role of public funding in politics. In fact, there is one measure, labelled as state dependency (Casal Bértoa et al., 2014). It reflects the share of state funding in the structure of party income. The higher the share of public funding, the higher the rate of state dependency. Considering that it is a measure derived from real data on public funding, it should be a better measure. While this is true, state dependency might still be a biased measure compared to the actual amount of subsidies per vote. Why so? The main reason is that the the amount of public funding could affect its own share in the structure of party income. The higher the level of state financial support to parties, the lower the incentives to seek private contributions. Moreover, state dependency could still hide considerable variation in public funding per vote despite similar shares in the structure of party income across countries.
      To test whether this is the case, one needs both measures: subsidies per vote and the state dependency rate. Unfortunately, I do not have data on the state dependency rate for post-communist regimes, given the lack of reliable data on private financing. Therefore, I borrow data from other cross-national studies that provide both indicators Nassmacher (2009). The relationship between subsidies per vote and state dependency, presented in Figure 2, depicts a mixed picture.2 Although subsidies per vote and state dependency are positively associated, the strength of the relationship is not sufficient to make them exchangeable.
Figure 2: Relationship between the level of DPF per voter and the share of DPF in the structure of party income
As one could notice, expert-based indices are poor substitutes to objective indicators of political financing. While much better, still the degree of state dependence is not sufficiently precise to be used as a substitute to the actual level of public funding. This evidence warns against the blind employment of such measurements to study political finance from a comparative perspective.

title: Direct public funding of political parties: between proxy measures and hard data (1)
text:
This overview represents a brief and somewhat technical discussion of my article published in Party Politics concerning the validity and reliability of various proxy measures of political financing regulations (PFR) and direct public funding (DPF) of political parties (Lipcean, 2021). Scholars commonly employ such proxies to assess their impact on political competition, party system stability, emergence and success of new parties, or political corruption. However, one legitimate concern relates to the suitability of these measures to investigate and gauge the effect of party and campaign funding rules on the phenomena and processes mentioned above. Another justified concern touches on the extent to which these proxies reflect the content of PFR.
      Considering that the money-politics relationship in contemporary democracies became a vividly debated topic, these concerns are not trivial. Therefore, when researchers develop and use such measures and make policy recommendations on the direction of political finance reforms based on their findings, it is paramount that they reflect the lay of the land of PFR. Moreover, the performance of such proxies in capturing the nature of PFR is particularly relevant since, in most cases, political finance reforms are designed to level the playing field among electoral competitors, minimise the risk of corruption or undue influence on policy-making via party and campaign contributions. Hence, the way how researchers arrive at conclusions regarding the best tools to address the democratic malaise stemming from the disproportionate influence of vested interests on the decision-making process is crucial for the validity of their findings and recommendations.
      In a nutshell, I argue that when it comes to large-N cross-national studies assessing the effect of PFR/DPF on political competition or corruption, unfortunately, scholars mostly resort to proxy measures that do not capture the reality and complexity of PFR accurately. Thus, such measures are not as good as they could be, given the actual content of PFR. This limitation is determined by the overwhelming reliance on what I call regulatory scope. By contrast, I argue that besides regulatory scope, one also needs to look at regulatory intensity or depth.
      To understand the difference between the two, I provide a simple example, which will illustrate my point. For instance, when someone analyses the impact of donations or public funding of political parties on corruption or the impact of campaign spending limits on the electoral playing field through the lenses of regulatory scope, she will only consider whether there are (or not) donation and spending limits or whether the state provides (or not) public funds to parties or candidates. Conversely, the focus on regulatory intensity goes further. It is concerned with how much a donor can contribute, a party or candidate can spend, or public funds are granted to political parties to alleviate their fundraising burden. Although the advantages of regulatory intensity against the regulatory scope are self-evident, the former is rarely used in large-N cross-national research on party funding.
      Below, I provide an illustration based on my dataset on direct public funding of political parties covering 27 post-communist regimes over three decades of transition 1990-2020.1 Hence, I will go through a few indicators to illustrate that regulatory scope is insufficient to understand how permissive a PFR is in limiting the manoeuvring room of political parties and candidates to amass and spend money for their regular or campaign activities. Most charts are adapted based on the article’s figures.
      Before that, however, I will illustrate that post-communist polities used various methods to determine the level of state subsidies. The choice of a given method might affect the predictability of institutional settings within which political competition occurs. Likewise, it might affect the discretion of political office holders to manipulate the rules in their favour in terms of amount, access and distribution of state funding. More stable and predictable rules on public funding create more equal conditions for electoral competition. By contrast, the lack of or vague regulation enables incumbents to manipulate the allocation mechanism more easily to achieve their electoral goals. Hence, based on the method of determining the level of direct state support to parties, post-communist polities can be clustered into three generic categories based on:
Figure 1 illustrates the DPF level by method and activity type. The boxplot width shows the number of observations, which means that in most cases, post-communist regimes opted to set the DPF level based on a dynamic economic indicator. Likewise, this method seems to be associated with the most generous funding, although for the statutory party financing, those countries that employed an ad-hoc method provided, alike, quite generous state funding to parties.
Figure 1: Variation in the DPF level across post-communist regimes by the method and timeframe 1990-2020
Another shortcoming of regulatory scope is that it cannot account for the variation in DPF when the state provides subsidies for party statutory and election activities. Generally speaking, there are three scenarios in this respect: the state grants subsidies, either for party routine operations or electioneering activities, or both. Yet, the amount of budgetary resources allotted for each type might differ substantially. For instance, the government could provide regular and election subsidies, albeit the total support might still be minimal. Conversely, the aggregate funding might be very generous even though only one subsidy type is granted.
      Figure 2 illustrates well this situation. It shows the relationship between the subsidy level for party statutory and election activities. As one may notice, all scenarios are present in different combinations. In some cases, like Montenegro and the Czech Republic, both kinds of subsidies are generous. In others, such as Estonia, Bulgaria or Slovenia, statutory funding has precedence over election financing. By contrast, election funding has priority over regular financing in Slovakia and, more recently, in Hungary.
Figure 2: Relationship between the DPF level for party statutory and election financing in election years 1990-2020
Besides the failure to capture these differences, any proxy measure reflecting only the regulatory scope will also fail to account for within-country variation in public funding. Hence, a subsidy increase or decrease over time will remain unnoticed by a dichotomous indicator (0 – absence of subsidies, 1 – presence of subsidies) or a composite measure including public funding. For instance, the changes in the level of state support might affect the incentive structure of political parties or candidates to engage in corruption. To understand the risks of relying on the regulatory scope alone, Figure 3 presents the public funding evolution and change over time from the early ’90 until 2020. Once again, data reveal a tremendous cross-national and within-country variation.
Figure 3: Cross-national and within-country change in public funding between 1990-2020
The purpose of this brief sketch was to warn about the risks entailed by the reliance on various proxies used in comparative research on party finance. As data shows, such proxies are inaccurate and biased in reflecting the actual amount of budgetary subventions provided by the state to political parties, which also applies to other dimensions of political financing such as donation and spending limits. In the next part I will show how alternative proxies such as expert evaluations cannot replace objective indicators.

title: The world upside down: delegitimising political finance regulation employing alternative corruption indices
text:
In this blog post, I replicate one of a few comparative cross-national studies on the effect of political financing regulations on political corruption (Casal Bértoa et al., 2014).1 In a nutshell, the title of the paper suggests that political financing regulations (PFR) do not live up to our expectations in reducing political corruption. Despite the normative belief that more party and campaign financing regulations should diminish political corruption, the authors come to a rather pessimistic conclusion. They do not find evidence that donation caps, public funding of political parties or punishments for financing-related breaches diminish corruption.
      Of course, their findings represent a heavy blow to policymakers’ efforts to curb political corruption by restricting the inflows and outflows of political money. The most disappointing result in their study relates to the lack of any curbing effect of state funding. This result is even more disappointing considering the fact that authors use a rather good instrument for measuring public funding of parties - state dependency rate. Here, state dependency represents the proportion of state subsidies in the structure of party income, which means the amount of money political parties receive directly from the state budget for running their regular and electoral activities. One would expect that the more funding parties get from the public purse, the less they will be tempted to ask for illegal funding, thus the lower the probability of getting entangled in corrupt transactions. Hence, Casal Bértoa et al. (2014) test this argument using information on state dependency rate, but fail to confirm this expectation.
      Yet, while they have a pretty good indicator of public funding, the corruption measure they selected is a more specific one - citizens perception of how corrupt political parties are from the Global Corruption Barometer (GCB) conducted by Transparency International. While nothing is wrong with choosing this indicator, one issue in many corruption studies is that the results might be considerably affected by the choice of corruption index. Although many corruption indices are highly correlated, this is not always the case when the index reflects citizens’ not experts’ perceptions about political corruption. This is why I replicate this study but also use alternative corruption measures. Among these alternatives, I look at some older indices widely used in cross-national research on corruption, such as the Corruption Perception Index (Transparency International) (CPI), Control of Corruption index (World Bank Governance Indicators) (WBGI) or International Country Risk Guide, and newer ones including political corruption index (V-DEM) from the Varieties of Democracies dataset (Coppedge et al., 2021; Maerz et al., 2021) and the Bayesian Corruption index (BCI) (Standaert, 2015). As Figure 1 shows, the correlation between almost all expert-based perception indices for countries used in Casal Bértoa et al. (2014) analysis is astonishingly high. But all of them display a visibly lower correlation with the GCB index.

title: Public Funding of Political Parties Is Unlikely To Reduce Corruption
text:
This blogpost was originally published on the Global Anticorruption Blog and is republished below.1
      Does public funding of political parties reduce corruption? Intuitively, there are good reasons to believe that it does. After all, when parties receive a substantial portion of their funding from public sources, they are less dependent on private contributions—both legal and illegal. That straightforward logic has led many scholars and prestigious organizations to recommend higher levels of public funding for parties and candidates. The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers, for example, recommends public funding of political parties and electoral candidates as an anticorruption measure, and the OECD, while not explicitly using the language of corruption, recommends public funding as part of a holistic system of political finance regulation to limit policy capture.

title: Party registration requirements in Moldova 1991-2020: a comparative outlook
text:
Evolution of party registration requirements
      Moldova’s journey in regulating party registration reveals a significant shift from liberal to restrictive requirements. When the Law on Parties and Other Socio-Political Organizations (LPSOP) was adopted in 1991, the registration process required only 300 signatures (Monitorul Oficial, Nr. 11-12, art. 106, 1991). However, the 1998 amendment marked a dramatic change, increasing the requirement to 5,000 members and introducing territorial distribution requirements (Monitorul Oficial, №. 100-102. art. 613, 1998). Specifically, parties needed members to reside in at least half of the second-level administrative-territorial units, with a minimum of 150 members in each. The 2008 Law on Political Parties (LPP) slightly moderated these requirements, reducing the minimum to 4,000 members and 120 members per district (Monitorul Oficial, №. 42-44, art. 119, 2008). However, as this analysis demonstrates, even these adjusted requirements remained notably stringent in a regional context.
Comparative analysis of registration requirements
      Figure 1 presents the minimum number of members required for party registration across post-communist regimes since the early 1990s. While Moldova ranks 13th in raw numbers, this metric alone provides an incomplete picture.








Figure 1: Cross-national and cross-temporal variation in party registration requirements (numbr of signatures) across post-communist regimes 1990-2019




      A more nuanced understanding emerges when we consider these requirements in relation to each country’s electoral market. Figure 2 illustrates this relationship by showing the ratio between registered voters and required members. This analysis reveals Moldova holds the third position in terms of stringency of registration requirements, trailing only behind Kazakhstan (2002-2019) and Slovakia (2005-2019).








Figure 2: Cross-national and cross-temporal variation in the stringency of party registration requirements across post-communist regimes 1990-2019




      In practical terms, a new party in Moldova needed to recruit one member from every 608 registered voters when the new LPP was adopted in 2008. This challenge becomes even more daunting when one considers migration and other voter related registration issues. Figure 3 provides an integrated perspective, combining the insights from Figures 1 and 2 to demonstrate how raw membership requirements and voter pool size interact to create varying levels of accessibility for new political parties across different countries. On the X-axis is shows the size of the voters’ pool in registered voters, on the Y-axis there are signature requirements while the size of the bubbles indicate the stringency of registration requirement. The larger the bubble the more effort newly aspiring political parties need to deploy to recruit potential members. As one may notice, Moldova is among those political regimes placing a heavier burden to achieve this goal.








Figure 3: Cross-national variation in the stringency of party registration requirements across post-communist regimes 1990-2019 relative to the size of voters’ pool and signature requirements




Territorial distribution requirements
      The territorial representation requirement introduced in 1998 added another significant barrier to party registration since they needed at least 120 members residing in half of the second-tier administrative units (districts). While the 1999 ruling of the Constitutional Court upheld this requirement, finding it consistent with freedom of association (Curtea Constituțională, 1999), it represents another hurdle for the emergence of new parties. The “territorial representation” requirement is less widespread across post-communist world. Out of 27 countries, only 10 have implemented such a rule, but Moldova’s version stands among the strictest. Figure 4 shows that among the ten post-communist countries that implemented territorial requirements, Moldova’s were among the most demanding, particularly when considering the size of its electorate. Only Romania imposed comparable territorial requirements, mandating at least 700 members in each of 18 counties. Notably, several countries have moved away from such requirements – Russia, for instance, abandoned territorial representation rules after 2012.








Figure 4: Cross-national variation in the stringency of party registration requirements based on territorial distribution of membership across post-communist regimes 1990-2019




A new constitutional shift
      A significant shift occurred in 2020 when Moldova’s Constitutional Court ruled that both the 4,000-member requirement and the territorial representation condition were excessively restrictive and unconstitutional (Curtea Constituțională, 2020). This landmark decision acknowledged that these requirements created disproportionate barriers to political participation and association.

Implications for democratic development

      This analysis demonstrates that Moldova’s party registration requirements, prior to the 2020 Constitutional Court decision, placed it among the most restrictive regimes in the post-communist space. The combined effect of high membership thresholds and territorial distribution requirements created substantial barriers to entry for new political forces, potentially hampering political pluralism and democratic development. The Court’s 2020 decision represents a significant step toward aligning Moldova’s party registration framework with democratic principles and regional best practices.This constitutional shift highlights the need to carefully calibrate party registration requirements: they must be robust enough to ensure genuine political commitment while remaining accessible enough to foster democratic pluralism, participation and competition.

title: Who funded Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary campaign? Donations and income structure
text:
The parliamentary elections of 28 September 2025 in Moldova were held under a tightened campaign finance framework. The amendments adopted in June 2025 (Monitorul Oficial, 2025) came after evidence of large-scale illicit financing and foreign interference around the 2024 presidential election and the EU accession referendum. In this post, the first of a few based on my analysis in the Moldovan Analytical Digest (Lipcean, 2026), I look at the income side of the campaign: how much money electoral contestants raised, which sources it came from, and how broad their donor bases were.
There is one caveat though. The analysis relies on the official financial reports that contestants filed with the Central Electoral Commission (CEC) through its online financial control platform (Comisia Electorală Centrală, 2025). It therefore says nothing about illicit or undeclared funding, which is by nature hard to measure. It can nevertheless show how legally declared resources are distributed, and that distribution is not equal.
The rules of the game
Individuals could contribute up to six average monthly wages (AMW; MDL 96,600, about €4,950) and legal entities up to twelve AMW (MDL 193,200, about €9,900). Cash donations were capped at one AMW (MDL 16,100, about €825), businesses could donate only by bank transfer, companies with outstanding debts to the state budget or insurance funds were barred from donating, and contestants could not accept in-kind donations without advance payment (Monitorul Oficial, 2022). Besides private money, contestants could move up to 70% of the state subsidies available in their party accounts into their election account. Throughout this post, amounts in euro are converted from lei at about MDL 19.5 per euro.
Who raised the money?
Taken together, the 21 contestants covered in the figures reported an income of about €5.0 million. Panel A of Figure 1 shows that this money was extremely concentrated. The Patriotic Electoral Bloc (BEP) and the Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS) each raised more than €1.2 million, followed by the Alternative Bloc (BEA) and Our Party (PN). These four contestants alone account for €4.11 million, or 82% of the total, while the remaining 17 contestants together raised €0.91 million. The best-funded bloc raised several hundred times more than the smallest contestants.
Figure 1: Campaign income of electoral contestants in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections, by income source. Panel A shows absolute amounts (the label is the net total income), panel B the share of each source.
Where did the money come from?
Panel B of Figure 1 reveals that the funding portfolios are as different as the amounts. Volunteer work, valued by the contestants themselves, is the single largest source of income overall (43% of everything reported), followed by donations from individuals (34%). Own private funds, donations from businesses, in-kind donations, and the state subsidies that parties transferred to their campaign accounts each account for much smaller shares.1
Behind these averages are different strategies. The incumbent PAS built a diversified portfolio: individual donations make up 36% of its reported income, volunteer work 28%, the party’s own private funds 17% and donations from businesses 15%. BEP, by contrast, relied on volunteers for 66% of its income and received no business donations at all. BEA and PN lean on individual donors (48% and 55%), complemented by volunteer work. Most of the smaller contestants depend on one or two sources, which leaves them financially vulnerable.
A striking contrast: individual versus corporate money
Business donations tell a different story from individual ones. Only two contestants collected substantial amounts from legal entities: PAS (€197,528) and the Moldovans Alliance (AM, €96,000). For PAS this is 15% of its income, but for AM it is 41%, which makes the party much more dependent on a few corporate donors. All other contestants together raised only €25,806 from businesses. Open corporate support is therefore a scarce resource, available mostly to the incumbent. Whether the money declared as donations from individuals sometimes hides corporate or other interests is a different question, which journalistic investigations have raised and which I discuss in the digest (Lipcean, 2026).
Donor networks: breadth versus depth
Totals do not tell us how contestants raised their funds. Figure 2 relates the total amount raised to the number of contributions, and the size of the point shows the average contribution. In the monetary donations (panel A), PAS has by far the broadest donor network, with 1,469 contributions at an average of only €313, the lowest of all contestants. This is what a grass-roots fundraising strategy looks like. BEA (455 contributions, average €739) and PN (425, €838) raised comparable totals with larger average donations, while BEP collected only 270 monetary contributions (average €540). At the other extreme, 9 of the 20 contestants reported fewer than 20 monetary contributions, while AM relied on just 20 donors giving on average €3,631.
Panel B shows an even larger disparity in volunteer work. BEP reported 22,833 volunteer contributions with a total value above €1 million, an average of only €46 each. PAS, the incumbent, reported less than half as many (9,595), followed by PN (2,719), MRM (1,542) and BEA (1,120). Most other contestants reported fewer than 100 contributions. Volunteer mobilisation thus amplifies rather than offsets organisational differences: well-funded contestants with strong structures mobilised thousands of supporters, while resource-poor contestants failed to engage even narrow volunteer pools.
Figure 2: Donor networks of electoral contestants in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections: total amount raised and number of contributions (both on log scales). The size and colour of each point show the average contribution in euro.
What this means for competition
The picture is one of a highly stratified playing field. A small group of well-established contestants raised sums that dwarfed those available to everyone else, and they could tap several sources at the same time: individual donations, business money, their own funds, and volunteer labour. Most of the others depended on one or two sources, usually small individual donations or a handful of volunteers. At the same time, the data show a more pluralistic fundraising landscape than one might expect. Even though PAS was the incumbent, it was not the only contestant to attract substantial private donations: BEA, PN and BEP also raised large amounts, and several contestants mobilised thousands of volunteers.
Whether this money translated into votes is a different matter, and I turn to it in a later post, after first looking at how contestants spent their funds.

title: How did Moldova’s parties spend their campaign money? Spending patterns in the 2025 elections
text:
This is the second post based on my analysis in the Moldovan Analytical Digest (Lipcean, 2026). After looking at how electoral contestants raised money in the 2025 parliamentary elections in Moldova, here I turn to the demand side: how much they spent, what they spent it on, and whether well-funded and resource-poor contestants spent differently. As before, the analysis uses the official financial reports that contestants filed with the Central Electoral Commission (CEC) (Comisia Electorală Centrală, 2025b), and therefore covers only declared spending. The figures cover the same 21 contestants as in the previous post.
How much did contestants spend?
The law capped the spending of each contestant at 0.1% of state budget revenues, which amounted to MDL 75,932,486, or about €3.9 million (Comisia Electorală Centrală, 2025a). This is roughly MDL 28 (€1.4) per registered voter. The cap was twice as high as a share of budget revenues as in the 2021 parliamentary elections (0.05%, or MDL 20,707,700 (Comisia Electorală Centrală, 2021)), and about 3.7 times higher in nominal terms. In practice, it was far from binding. The biggest spender, the Patriotic Electoral Bloc (BEP), used 41% of the cap, and the incumbent Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS) 33%. Most contestants spent less than 2% of it.
Contestants together reported spending of about €5.0 million. The ranking is therefore the same as for income, and reported spending matches reported income almost to the euro for every contestant (the largest difference is about €10). The inequalities in funding that I described in the previous post carry over one-to-one into spending, and the interesting question is how contestants allocated what they had.
Where did the money go?
Figure 1 breaks spending down into its categories. Three categories dominate: volunteer activities (44% of all reported spending), broadcast advertisements (25%) and promotional materials (19%). Together they make up 89% of everything contestants spent. The remaining categories are small: in-kind goods and services account for 5%, transport for 2%, while premises, personnel and legal fees are each below 0.5%.








Figure 1: Campaign spending of electoral contestants in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections, by spending category. Panel A shows absolute amounts (the label is the net total spending), panel B the share of each category. The three largest categories are shown separately, all others are grouped.

Volunteers: the most fungible resource
Volunteer work is the largest spending item, and it is the one that links the two sides of the campaign budget: it is both an income (what supporters contribute) and an expense (what the contestant reports as the value of their work). This is also the category where the gap between contestants is widest. For BEP, volunteer activities are 66% of reported spending, and for the Respect Moldova Movement (MRM) 57%. For the incumbent PAS the share is 28%. Most smaller contestants report little or no volunteer spending at all. The capacity to deploy volunteers is, in other words, itself a marker of organisational strength.
What do volunteers do? In the digest I use the disaggregated volunteer reports to show that about three quarters of volunteer activities, around 30,000 instances, consisted of distributing promotional materials through direct contact with voters. Beyond this canvassing effort, over 6,000 representatives staffed polling stations, while the remaining volunteers provided media, logistics and operational support (Lipcean, 2026).
Broadcast advertisements and promotional materials
Broadcast advertisements are the second spending pillar, and here the picture reverses. PAS spent €503,710 on producing and airing commercials, 39% of its spending, more than any other contestant in absolute terms. The other big spenders chose differently: BEP devoted only 7% of its spending to commercials, BEA 26% and PN 31%. Among the smaller contestants, commercials were typically a larger share of the budget than for the big ones: outside the six best-funded contestants, the median share of spending on broadcast advertisements is 46%. Several of them spent more than two thirds of their entire budget on it. Paid advertising seems to be the way in which resource-poor contestants try to compensate for their lack of organisation, because it buys visibility without requiring a network of volunteers.
Promotional materials, such as printed leaflets and posters, are the third category. Their shares are more balanced among the best-funded contestants: they take between 13% and 37% of the spending of each of the six best-funded contestants, which suggests that printed materials are a baseline investment for contestants with an established organisation.
Figure 2 puts the two main strategies side by side. Each point is a contestant, placed by the share of its spending that went to volunteer activities (horizontal axis) and to broadcast advertisements (vertical axis), with the size of the point showing total spending. The contestants spread along a diagonal from “advertisement-only” campaigns in the upper left to volunteer-heavy ones in the lower right. The top contestants are not at the same place on it: BEP and MRM are volunteer-driven, PAS and PN are in the middle, and most small contestants are at the top left.








Figure 2: Campaign spending strategies of electoral contestants in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections: share of spending on volunteer activities and on broadcast advertisements. The size of the point shows total spending.





What this means for competition
Spending patterns mirror the revenue patterns: a bifurcated landscape. Top-tier contestants could pursue different strategies, balancing grassroots operations, media presence and organisational infrastructure, and each of them chose a different mix. Resource-constrained contestants faced a much narrower choice, and concentrated their funds on visibility-enhancing activities such as paid commercials, since their organisations could not offset a lack of money with volunteers. Even the best-funded contestant stayed far below the legal spending cap, which therefore played little role in limiting the campaign.
Whether any of this spending translated into votes is the question for the next post.

title: Does spending more money win more votes? Moldova’s 2025 elections
text:
This is the third post based on my analysis in the Moldovan Analytical Digest (Lipcean, 2026). In the first two I looked at how the parties and candidates in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections raised money and how they spent it. Here I ask the obvious next question: did those who spent more money also get more votes?
The short answer is yes, but only at the top. Contestants with small budgets got very few votes, whatever they spent. Those with big budgets got a lot more, and each extra euro seemed to buy more votes than the one before. But with only 21 contestants, nobody can say exactly how much money it takes.
What the data look like
Figure 1 shows each contestant’s spending and the share of votes it got. I measure spending in two ways: total spending, which includes the value of the work done by volunteers, and monetary spending, which counts only the money actually spent. The figure uses total spending. It is drawn on a logarithmic scale (each step to the right is a multiplication, not an addition), because spending varies from less than €2,000 to more than €1.5 million. The dashed line is the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament.
Contestants that spent more generally got more votes, and the four biggest spenders all got more than 5%. But there is a lot of scatter. The Democracy at Home Party (PDA) passed the threshold with only about €12,500, while the Respect Moldova Movement (MRM) spent more than €300 thousand and got less than 1%.








Figure 1: Campaign spending and vote share of electoral contestants in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections. Spending includes the value of volunteer work and is shown on a logarithmic scale. The dashed line is the 5% threshold.





How many votes does spending go with?
To see the overall pattern behind the dots, I fitted a statistical model to the data. Instead of drawing one single line through the dots, it draws thousands of possible lines that are all reasonable given the data. The solid line in Figure 2 is the middle one, and the shaded bands show where most of the other lines fall (50%, 80% and 95% of them). A narrow band means we are fairly sure, and a wide band means we are not.
The curve is flat at first and then bends sharply upwards. A contestant spending €100 thousand is expected to get about 2.2% of the votes (most likely between 1.1% and 4.6%). With €500 thousand the expected share is about 8.7% (between 5.7% and 13.3%). The bands get wider as spending grows, because only a few contestants have large budgets, so we are least sure just where the stakes are highest. When we count only money actually spent, the curve is steeper: €500 thousand of monetary spending goes with about 17.6% of the votes. The small rise at the far left of the curves is a quirk of the method and can be ignored.








Figure 2: Expected vote share by spending level in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections. The line is the middle estimate, the bands show where 50%, 80% and 95% of the possible curves fall. Points are the contestants; the dashed line is the 5% threshold. Curves stop at the highest spending observed for each measure.





Does each extra euro buy more votes?
The bend in the curve means that the more a contestant already spends, the more votes an extra euro seems to buy. To see this, imagine a contestant that doubles its spending. If it starts at €25 thousand, doubling to €50 thousand goes with an increase of only about 0.3 percentage points in the vote share. If it starts at €200 thousand, doubling to €400 thousand goes with about 3.2 percentage points. In other words, votes are not bought at a fixed price: extra spending barely moves the needle for small contestants and matters much more for big ones. This fits the idea that large budgets give access to expensive but effective tools, such as television advertising and professional campaigns, that small budgets cannot buy.
What were the chances of getting into parliament?
The curve in Figure 2 is an average. What a contestant actually gets also depends on things the model cannot see: how well organised it is, how well known, how good its candidates are, and plain luck. Figure 3 takes this into account and shows, for each spending level, the chance of getting at least 5% of the votes.
Spending a lot makes success likely. Spending little makes it unlikely, but not impossible. With €100 thousand of total spending the chance is about 15%, with €300 thousand it is 40%, and with €500 thousand it is 68%. Even for the smallest budgets the chance is around 7%, which fits the case of PDA: unlikely, but it happened.
So how much does a contestant need to spend before it can expect to reach 5%? The model’s middle estimate is about €282 thousand of total spending, but it could plausibly be anywhere between €111 thousand and €449 thousand. For money actually spent, the middle estimate is about €208 thousand (between €119 and €275 thousand). The wide ranges are the real message: with 21 contestants we can say that getting into parliament takes a substantial budget, but not exactly how much. As a check, the standard method with a single best-fit curve gives a similar answer, about €301 thousand for total spending and about €213 thousand for monetary spending.








Figure 3: Chance of getting at least 5% of the votes by spending level in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections. The curve is averaged over all the possible curves of the model.





What this does not tell us
These numbers show how spending and votes go together in this election. They do not prove that spending causes votes. A popular party can attract both money and votes, and with only 21 contestants I cannot take into account other things that matter a lot, such as being the party in government, party organisation, media coverage and name recognition. The figures also only cover officially declared spending, not illicit money, which by its nature is hard to measure.
Bottom line
More spending went with more votes, but not in a straight line. Small budgets bought almost nothing, a contestant needed a substantial budget to have a realistic chance of reaching 5%, and for those who already had a lot of money, each extra euro seemed to count for more. But money was neither a guarantee nor strictly necessary: some big spenders fell short, and one small spender got into parliament.






NoteFor the technically minded





The model is a Bayesian beta regression (a standard method for percentages) fitted with the brms package (Bürkner, 2017; see also Ferrari & Cribari-Neto, 2004; Grün et al., 2012). The vote share depends on spending through a curve (a quadratic term in standardised log spending), and I estimate it separately for total and monetary spending. I use weakly informative priors, Normal(0, 1) for the coefficients, and four chains of 5,000 iterations. The largest R-hat is 1.002 and there were 0 divergent transitions, so the estimation worked without problems. I chose this curved specification over a straight line, and over a version where the spread of vote shares changes with spending, because it predicted best or equally well for both measures when I left each contestant out in turn. Official data on spending and results come from the Central Electoral Commission (Comisia Electorală Centrală, 2025b, 2025a).












References

Bürkner, P.-C. (2017). Brms: An R package for Bayesian multilevel models using Stan. Journal of Statistical Software, 80(1), 1–28.


Comisia Electorală Centrală. (2025a). Pentru aprobarea Raportului cu privire la rezultatele alegerilor parlamentare din 28 septembrie 2025. https://a.cec.md/ro/pentru-aprobarea-raportului-cu-privire-la-rezultatele-alegerilor-parlamentare-di-2751_115477.html


Comisia Electorală Centrală. (2025b). Sistemul informatic “Control financiar”. https://finante.cec.md/reports.aspx


Ferrari, S., & Cribari-Neto, F. (2004). Beta regression for modelling rates and proportions. Journal of Applied Statistics, 31(7), 799–815.


Grün, B., Kosmidis, I., & Zeileis, A. (2012). Extended beta regression in R: Shaken, stirred, mixed, and partitioned. Journal of Statistical Software, 48, 1–25.


Lipcean, S. (2026). Campaign financing in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections. Moldovan Analytical Digest, 5, 2–17. https://doi.org/10.3929/ethz-c-000793910

title: Who funded Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary campaign? Donations and income structure
text:
The parliamentary elections of 28 September 2025 in Moldova were held under stricter campaign finance rules. The amendments passed in June 2025 (Monitorul Oficial, 2025) were a response to large-scale illegal financing and foreign interference around the 2024 presidential election and the EU accession referendum. In this post, the first of a few based on my analysis in the Moldovan Analytical Digest (Lipcean, 2026), I look at the income side of the parliamentary campaign: how much money the contestants raised, where it came from, how many contributions they received and how these were distributed among the donor pool.
There is one caveat that should be mentioned. The analysis relies on the official financial reports that contestants filed with the Central Electoral Commission (CEC) through its online financial control platform (Comisia Electorală Centrală, 2025). It therefore says nothing about illicit or undeclared funding, which is by nature hard to measure. It can nevertheless reveal how legally declared resources are distributed among contestants, and that distribution is far from equal.
The rules of the game
During this campaign, individuals could contribute up to six average monthly wages (AMW; MDL 96,600, about €4,950), while legal entities up to twelve AMW (MDL 193,200, about €9,900).1 Cash donations were capped at one AMW (MDL 16,100, about €825), businesses could donate only by bank transfer, companies with outstanding debts to the state budget or social security and health insurance funds were barred from donating. Moreover, electoral competitors could not accept in-kind donations without advance payment (Monitorul Oficial, 2022). Besides private money, contestants could move up to 70% of the state subsidies available in their party accounts into their election account.
Who raised the money?
Collectively, the 21 electoral contestants collected about €5.0 million of reported income. Panel A of Figure 1 shows that this money was extremely concentrated. The Patriotic Electoral Bloc (BEP) and the Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS) each raised more than €1.2 million, followed by the Alternative Bloc (BEA) and Our Party (PN). These four contestants alone account for €4.11 million, or 82% of the total, while the remaining 17 collected together €0.91 million. The best-funded bloc raised several hundred times more than the smallest contestants.
Figure 1 has two panels that show the structure of campaign income in absolute and relative terms. Panel A displays the ranking of electoral contestants from the largest to the smallest in terms of total income and its distribution by funding source, while Panel B displays the share of each income source from the total income.
Figure 1: Campaign income of electoral contestants in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections, by income source. Panel A shows absolute amounts (the label is the net total income), panel B the share of each source.
Where did the money come from?
Panel B of Figure 1 shows that contestants also relied on very different sources of money. Volunteer work, valued by the contestants themselves, is the largest income source (43% of everything reported), followed by donations from individuals (34%). Own funds, donations from businesses, in-kind donations and state subsidies that parties moved to their campaign accounts each make up much smaller shares.2
Behind these totals are different strategies. For instance, PAS, the party in government, exhibits a relatively balanced income structure collecting funding from several sources: individual donations make up 36% of its reported income, volunteer work 28%, its own funds 17% and donations from businesses 15%. BEP, by contrast, relied heavily on volunteers for 66% of its income and received no business donations at all. BEA and PN relied mostly on individual donors (48% and 55%), plus volunteer work. Most smaller contestants exhibit less balanced budgets, depending on one or two sources, which left them financially vulnerable.
The scarcity of business money
The shortage of business donations is reflected by the fact that only two contestants collected large amounts from businesses: PAS (€197,528) and the Moldovans Alliance (AM, €96,000). For PAS this represents 15% of its income, whereas for AM it constitutes 41%, so AM depended much more on business money. All other contestants collectively amassed only €25,806 from businesses. Business money was therefore scarce, and went mostly to the party in government. A question still remains, whether some business contributions were disguised and reported as individual donations. Some journalists have raised this issue, for instance here, and I touch upon it in the digest (Lipcean, 2026).
Donor pool and donation value
Totals do not show how contestants raised their money, so Figure 2 plots, for each contestant, the total amount raised (x-axis) against the number of contributions it received (y-axis) by the size of average donation. Both axes use a logarithmic scale to show both small and large values in the same plot. The size and colour of each point show the average contribution by electoral contestant. Panel A covers monetary donations, while panel B volunteer contributions. As panel A shows, PAS has by far the largest donor pool, 1,469, with an average of only €313 – the lowest donation value among contestants. This reflects a grass-roots fundraising strategy, that is, raising money from many small donors. BEA (455 contributions, average €739) and PN (425, €838) raised comparable amounts with larger average donations, while BEP collected only 270 monetary contributions (average €540). At the other end, 9 of the 20 contestants reported fewer than 20 monetary contributions. Notably, while AM received only 20 donations, it recorded the largest average donation per donor of €3,631.
Panel B shows even bigger gaps in volunteer work. BEP reported 22,833 volunteer contributions with a total value above €1 million, an average of only €46 each. PAS, the party in government, reported less than half as many (9,595), followed by PN (2,719), MRM (1,542) and BEA (1,120). Most other contestants reported fewer than 100 contributions. Hence, the volunteer activity widens the gap between contestants instead of closing them: well-funded contestants with strong organisations mobilised thousands of supporters, while those with little money reached a very narrow pool of volunteers.
Figure 2: Donor networks of electoral contestants in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections: total amount raised and number of contributions (both on log scales). The size and colour of each point show the average contribution in euro.
What this means for competition
The playing field was very uneven. A small group of well-established contestants raised far more than everyone else, and they used several sources at the same time: individual donations, business money, their own funds and volunteers. Most of the others depended on one or two sources, usually small individual donations or a handful of volunteers. At the same time, the money was not concentrated in a single party. PAS, the party in government, was not the only one to raise large amounts: BEA, PN and BEP did too, and several contestants mobilised thousands of volunteers.
Did this money turn into votes? I come back to this in a later post, after looking at how contestants spent their money.

title: Does spending more money win more votes? Moldova’s 2025 elections
text:
This is the third post based on my analysis in the Moldovan Analytical Digest (Lipcean, 2026). The first and second posts examined how the parties and candidates in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections gathered their campaign funds and how they spent them, so here I turn to the question that naturally follows: did the contestants with the deepest pockets also obtain the most votes?
The short answer is yes, but mainly at the top of the spending ladder. Contestants running on a very limited budget attracted very few votes, whereas the big spenders secured far more. In addition, the more funding a contestant had already invested, the more support each additional euro appeared to bring. With only 21 contestants, however, it is nearly impossible to say precisely how much money one needed to invest for a given vote share.

A preliminary glance of the data
Figure 1 plots, for each contestant, how much it spent against the share of the votes it obtained. I measure spending in two ways: monetary spending, which counts only the cash actually spent and total spending, which also includes the value of activities carried out by volunteers. Figure 1 presents the information on total spending. Since spending varies enormously, from less than €2,000 to more than €1.5 million, the x-axis uses a logarithmic scale, thus helping to show small and large spenders against their vote shares in the same picture. Each dot is a contestant, and the dashed red line marks the 5% threshold required to enter parliament, so the green dots above the line are the contestants that cleared the electoral threshold.
Overall, contestants that spent more gained more votes, while the four biggest spenders all surpassed 5%. Yet the picture is not as clear as one may expect. For instance, the Democracy at Home Party (PDA) cleared the threshold with only about €12,500, while the Moldovans Alliance (AM) and Respect Moldova Movement (MRM) poured about €235 thousand and €300 thousand into their campaign chests respectively, but collected less than 1% of the votes.








Figure 1: Campaign spending and vote share of electoral contestants in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections. Spending includes the value of volunteer work and is shown on a logarithmic scale. The dashed line is the 5% threshold.





How many votes does spending go with?
To uncover the overall pattern behind the dots in Figure 1, I fitted a Bayesian beta regression to the data, which is a model suited to outcomes that are proportions, like the vote share in our case. A key difference from a standard Beta regression is that instead of estimating a single best-fit line, the Bayesian model generates thousands of plausible lines consistent with the data. Figure 2 shows these lines for total and monetary spending. The solid line is the median of those plausible lines produced by the model, while the shaded bands show the ranges containing 50%, 80%, and 95% of them.
A contestant spending €100 thousand is expected to obtain about 2.3% of the votes (most likely between 1.1% and 4.5%), whereas with €500 thousand the expected share increases to about 8.7% (between 5.6% and 13.4%). The model is more uncertain at high spending levels, simply because fewer contestants spent large amounts relative to more contestants that spent much less. If one takes only monetary spending, €500 thousand corresponds to roughly 17.6% of the votes.








Figure 2: Expected vote share by spending level in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections. The line is the middle estimate, the bands show where 50%, 80% and 95% of the possible curves fall. Points are the contestants; the dashed line is the 5% threshold. Curves stop at the highest spending observed for each measure.





Does each extra euro buy more votes?
The steepening of the curve implies that the more a contestant has already spent, the more votes an additional euro appears to buy. To illustrate, consider a contestant that doubles its spending and ask how much its vote share would increase. Figure 3 answers this for five starting levels, from €25,000 to €400,000. Each marker depicts the range of plausible gains in percentage points: the dot is the middle estimate, the thick and thin lines contain 80% and 95% of the plausible values, and the dashed line marks no change.
A contestant starting at €25 thousand that doubles its budget to €50 thousand gains only about 0.3 percentage points in vote share, whereas one starting at €200 thousand and doubling to €400 thousand gains about 3.2 percentage points. In other words, votes are not bought at a fixed price: extra spending has little effects on electoral gains at lower spending levels but matters far more at higher ones. This somewhat sustains the idea that large budgets unlock expensive but effective campaign tools, such as TV advertising and professional campaigns, that small budgets cannot afford. Yet, as the Figure 3 shows, the model is also significantly more uncertain about the size of electoral gains at higher spending levels as illustrated by a wider range of plausible values for the well-funded contestants.








Figure 3: Change in expected vote share (percentage points) when spending doubles, starting from different spending levels in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections (dot: middle estimate; thick and thin lines: 80% and 95% plausible ranges).





What were the chances of getting into parliament?
The curve in Figure 2 is the model’s central estimate of the vote share, depending exclusively on the money spent. However, electoral success and actual votes a contestant obtains also hinges on factors the model does not know, including the quality of the contestants, public recognition, whether they are in government or in opposition or plain luck. Figure 4 takes this uncertainty into account and shows, for each spending level, the chance of winning at least 5% of the votes.
For instance, contestants spending €100 thousand have a chance of clearing electoral threshold of about 15%, for those spending €300 thousand the chance jumps to 41%, while with €500 thousand it increases to 68%. Even contestants with the smallest budgets have a chance of passing the threshold of around 7%, which fits the case of PDA - a highly unlikely case, but it happened.








Figure 4: Chance of getting at least 5% of the votes by spending level in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections. The curve is averaged over all the possible curves of the model.





So how much does a contestant need to spend before it can expect to reach 5%? Each of the thousands of possible curves crosses the 5% line at a different spending level, and Figure 5 shows how these spending levels are spread out. The black dot is the middle estimate, the thick and thin lines contain 80% and 95% of the possible values, while the dashed vertical line shows the estimate of a simpler beta model, which generates very close estimates, at about €301 thousand for the total spending model and about €213 thousand for the monetary spending one. Hence, the Bayesian model gives slightly lower estimates of the spending needed to reach 5% than the simpler beta model, although the difference is small compared with the range of plausible values.
For the total spending (left-hand panel), the middle estimate is about €289 thousand, but it could plausibly lie anywhere between €108 thousand and €443 thousand. For the monetary spending model (right-hand panel), the middle estimate is about €208 thousand (between €129 and €275 thousand). Given the wide range of plausible spending values, with 21 contestants it is hard to say accurately how much money a competitor needed to spend to clear the electoral threshold. Yet we know from the data that it required a rather hefty campaign budget.








Figure 5: Spending level beyond which the expected vote share stays above 5%, in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections. The distribution is from the Bayesian model (dot: middle estimate; thick and thin lines: 80% and 95% plausible ranges). The dashed line represents the estimate from a simple beta regression model.





What this does not tell us
These numbers show how spending and votes moved together in this parliamentary contest, but they do not prove that more spending did attract more votes. A popular party can attract both money and votes, and with only 21 contestants and money as a single factor, one cannot be certain about its role. Other factors, such as holding government office, party organisation, media coverage and name recognition matter a lot and we have not accounted for them. Moreover, these figures cover only officially declared spending, not illicit funds, which by their nature are hard to measure.
To conclude, while more spending went hand in hand with more votes, this relationship was not linear. Small campaign budgets yielded almost no electoral returns and a substantial war chest was needed for a realistic chance of clearing the 5% threshold. Moreover at already high spending levels, each additional euro appeared to matter more. But money was not a guarantee for electoral success, since some relatively big spenders fell short and a modest one managed to get into parliament.






NoteTechnical note





The model is a Bayesian beta regression, a method designed for outcomes that are percentages, such as vote shares. I estimated it with the brms package for R (Bürkner, 2017; see also Ferrari & Cribari-Neto, 2004; Grün et al., 2012), separately for total and for monetary spending. It lets the effect of spending change with the spending level, so that small and big budgets are not forced to follow the same straight line. I chose this set-up after testing simpler and more flexible alternatives: I left each contestant out in turn, checked how well each version predicted that contestant’s vote share, and this one predicted best, or as well as the others, for both measures. The model starts from deliberately vague assumptions, so that the data and not my own expectations drive the results, and I checked that the estimation ran without problems. The data on spending and election results come from the Central Electoral Commission (Comisia Electorală Centrală, 2025b, 2025a).

title: How did Moldova’s parties spend their campaign money? Spending patterns in the 2025 elections
text:
This is the second post based on my analysis in the Moldovan Analytical Digest (Lipcean, 2026). The first post looked at how contestants raised money in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections. Here I look at the other side: how much they spent, what they spent it on, and whether contestants with a lot of money spent differently from those with little. As before, the analysis uses the official financial reports that contestants filed with the Central Electoral Commission (CEC) (Comisia Electorală Centrală, 2025b), and therefore covers only declared spending. The figures cover the same 21 contestants as in the previous post.

How much did contestants spend?
The law capped each contestant’s spending at 0.1% of state budget revenues: MDL 75,932,486, or about €3.9 million (Comisia Electorală Centrală, 2025a). That is roughly MDL 28 (€1.4) per registered voter. In the 2021 elections the cap was half as large as a share of the budget (0.05%, or MDL 20,707,700 (Comisia Electorală Centrală, 2021)), so the 2025 cap was about 3.7 times higher in lei. In practice, nobody came close to it. The biggest spender, the Patriotic Electoral Bloc (BEP), used 41% of the cap, and the Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS), the party in government, 33%. Most contestants spent less than 2%.
Together, electoral competitors reported about €5.0 million in campaign spending. Given the interchangeability of income and spending totals, reported spending matches reported income almost to the euro (the largest difference is about €10), so the ranking is the same as for income. The inequality in fundraising described in the previous post is therefore also an inequality in spending. The interesting question is how contestants allocated their campaign money for different purposes to win the voters’ hearts and endorsement.
Where did the money go?
Figure 1 breaks spending down into four broad categories. Panel A ranks contestants based on spending budgets from the largest to the smallest. It also shows the distribution of spending categories in absolute numbers. Panel B displays the distribution of spending categories in percentage, which provides a more nuanced perspective on how contestants prioritised the allocation of campaign money for different purposes. To keep the figure readable, I show the three largest categories separately and lump all the others together. The three categories that dominate spending priorities include: volunteer activities (44% of all reported spending), broadcast advertisements (25%) and promotional materials (19%). Together they account for 89% of all campaign spending. The remaining categories are insignificant: in-kind goods and services account for 5%, transport for 2%, while premises, personnel and legal fees are each below 0.5%.








Figure 1: Campaign spending of electoral contestants in Moldova’s 2025 parliamentary elections, by spending category. Panel A shows absolute amounts (the label is the net total spending), panel B the share of each category. The three largest categories are shown separately, all others are grouped.





Volunteers
Volunteer work represents the largest spending item and is reported on both sides of the campaign budget, as income (what supporters contribute) and as spending (the value of their work, as reported by the contestant). This is also the category where the gap between electoral contestants is widest. For BEP, volunteer activities make up 66% of reported spending, and for the Respect Moldova Movement (MRM) 57%. For PAS, the party in government, it accounts for 28% of expenses. The majority of smaller contestants report little or no volunteer activity at all. We know that the ability to mobilize volunteers is a sign of relatively strong organisation.
What type of work did volunteers carry out? In the digest I used the detailed campaign reports of each contestant to show that about three quarters of volunteer activities, around 30,000 in all, consisted in handing out campaign materials in direct contact with voters. More than 6,000 worked as representatives at polling stations, and the rest helped with media, logistics and other support (Lipcean, 2026).
Broadcast advertisements and promotional materials
Broadcast advertisements are the second biggest item, and here the picture is different. PAS spent €503,710 on producing and airing commercials, 39% of its spending, more than any other contestant in euros. The other big spenders had other priorities: BEP devoted only 7% of its spending to commercials, BEA 26% and PN 31%. Among the less well-funded contestants, commercials were typically a larger share of the budget than for their wealthier counterparts. Outside the six best-funded contestants, the typical share spent on broadcast advertisements revolves around 46%, although several of them spent on broadcasting ads more than two thirds of their entire budget. Paid commercials were regarded by electoral competitors with little resources and limited organisation capacity to get campaign visibility to offset the shortage of a volunteer network.
Promotional materials, such as printed leaflets and posters, constitute the third spending category. Across the six best-funded contestants, they account for between 13% and 37% of spending, which suggests that such outlays are a routine cost for contestants with an established organisational structure.

What this means for competition
Given that campaign spending represents the flip side of fundraising, it reflects the same disparities in resources: several contestants spent considerably more than most of other competitors. The top-tier spenders had more options regarding how to allocate their funds between different categories. However, as data show, they had different preferences on how to combine volunteer work, media coverage and organisation. In contrast, contestants with limited funds had a much narrower choice. Without an extensive organisation and a narrow volunteer pool, they channeled most of their money into paid commercials to increase visibility.
These resource disparities raise a critical question: do they ultimately translate into votes? I provide a tentative answer in the next post.
